bishopric-of-dorpat.t: Prince-bishopric of south-eastern Estonia centred on Dorpat (Tartu), a prosperous Hanseatic frontier facing Pskov, until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1558.
bishopric-of-dorpat.o: Hermann of Buxhoeveden, brother of Bishop Albert of Riga, became bishop of the Estonians in 1220 and moved his see to Dorpat after its capture in 1224. The bishopric took over the former lands of Ugandi, Vaiga and Mõhu, and Hermann received them as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire.
bishopric-of-dorpat.r: The bishop ruled through a cathedral chapter and German vassals, sharing power with the Livonian Order and the diets of Terra Mariana. Dorpat, a Hanseatic member, grew rich from trade with Pskov and Novgorod and built a large Gothic cathedral. Estonian peasants worked the land under increasing serfdom.
bishopric-of-dorpat.e: At the start of the Livonian War Ivan IV of Russia took Dorpat in 1558, and the last bishop, Hermann Wesel, was taken to Russia, where he died. The territory was later contested by Poland-Lithuania and Sweden, and passed to Swedish Livonia in the 1620s.

belli.t: The Celtiberian people of Segeda, whose new city walls provoked the Roman war of 153 BCE and so moved the start of the Roman year to January.
belli.o: The Belli lived in the Jalón and Huerva valleys of modern Zaragoza province from about the 4th century BCE, part of the wider Celtiberian world. Their towns included Segeda and Contrebia Belaisca, the modern Botorrita.
belli.r: They lived in walled towns with councils of elders and magistrates. The Botorrita bronzes, the longest texts in the Celtiberian language, come from Contrebia Belaisca and record local regulations, while a Latin bronze from the same site records a Roman arbitration of 87 BCE. Their economy rested on farming, herding and metalworking.
belli.e: In 154 BCE Segeda enlarged its walls, which Rome treated as a breach of treaty. To send an army quickly, Rome began the consular year on 1 January 153 BCE. Led by Carus of Segeda, the Celtiberians defeated the consul Nobilior, but after Numantia fell in 133 BCE the Belli were absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

bavarian-soviet-republic.t: Short-lived council republic in Munich in April 1919, crushed by government troops and Freikorps in a wave of violence.
bavarian-soviet-republic.o: After the murder of Bavarian premier Kurt Eisner in February 1919, the elected government of Johannes Hoffmann fled Munich to Bamberg. On 6-7 April 1919 a council republic was proclaimed by writers and anarchists, including Ernst Toller, Erich Mühsam and Gustav Landauer.
bavarian-soviet-republic.r: The first council government was chaotic; within a week the Communists under Eugen Leviné took over and formed a Red Army. They decreed the socialisation of banks and industry and seized hostages. Supplies to Munich broke down. The killing of hostages at the Luitpold Gymnasium on 30 April inflamed opinion against the regime.
bavarian-soviet-republic.e: Government troops and Freikorps units entered Munich on 1-3 May 1919, killing several hundred people, including Landauer. Leviné was executed. The episode pushed Bavarian politics sharply to the right.

berbice.t: A Dutch plantation colony on the Berbice river in Guyana, remembered above all for the great slave uprising of 1763.
berbice.o: In 1627 the Zeeland merchant Abraham van Peere received a charter from the Dutch West India Company to settle the Berbice river. The colony began as a trading post at Fort Nassau upriver and was run as a private patroonship by the van Peere family.
berbice.r: Berbice developed sugar, coffee and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans. After a French raid in 1712, the colony was ransomed and from 1720 run by the Society of Berbice, a company of investors. In 1763 enslaved people led by Coffy rose up, controlled most of the colony for nearly a year and were suppressed only with outside troops. New Amsterdam later became the capital.
berbice.e: Britain occupied Berbice from 1796 and gained it formally in 1814. In 1831 it was merged with Demerara-Essequibo to form British Guiana. Coffy is Guyana's national hero, and 23 February, the start of the uprising, is the country's Republic Day.

boeotian-league.t: Federal state of the Boeotian cities under Theban leadership, which briefly made Thebes the strongest power in Greece after Leuctra in 371 BCE.
boeotian-league.o: The cities of Boeotia shared a dialect, cults and a sense of kinship, and by the late 6th century BCE Thebes was gathering them into a federation, an effort Plataea resisted by allying with Athens. After Boeotians fought on the Persian side in 479 BCE the league lapsed, and it was refounded after the defeat of Athens at Coronea in 447 BCE.
boeotian-league.r: The Hellenica Oxyrhynchia describes its 5th-century constitution: Boeotia was divided into eleven districts, each supplying a boeotarch, sixty federal councillors, soldiers and taxes in proportion, with Thebes holding four shares. Member cities kept local councils of propertied citizens. The federal coinage carried the Boeotian shield.
boeotian-league.e: The King's Peace dissolved it in 386 BCE, but Pelopidas and Epaminondas revived it after 379 BCE and defeated Sparta at Leuctra. Alexander destroyed Thebes in 335 BCE; a Hellenistic league continued until Rome dissolved it in 171 BCE.

banate-of-leitha.t: State proclaimed by Hungarian irregulars in 1921 to stop the transfer of Burgenland to Austria, whose resistance led to the plebiscite that kept Sopron Hungarian.
banate-of-leitha.o: The peace treaties of Saint-Germain and Trianon assigned German-speaking western Hungary, later called Burgenland, to Austria. When the handover began in August 1921, Hungarian irregulars of the Ragged Guard attacked Austrian gendarmes. On 4 October 1921 their commander, Pál Prónay, proclaimed the independent Banate of Leitha at Oberwart.
banate-of-leitha.r: The banate was a military occupation run by the irregulars, with a provisional administration and its own stamps; the Hungarian government officially disowned it while using it as a bargaining chip. Its population was mostly German-speaking, with Croatian and Hungarian minorities.
banate-of-leitha.e: Under Italian mediation the Venice Protocol of October 1921 agreed a plebiscite in Sopron, and the irregulars withdrew in November. Burgenland passed to Austria, while Sopron voted in December 1921 to stay in Hungary.

banate-of-severin.t: Hungarian frontier province at the Iron Gates of the Danube, a defensive march against Bulgarians, Cumans and later the Ottomans.
banate-of-severin.o: King Andrew II's son Béla set up the banate around 1228–1233, in lands taken from Bulgaria and the Cumans east of the Iron Gates, around the fortress of Severin (Drobeta-Turnu Severin) built on Roman ruins. In 1247 Béla IV granted it to the Knights Hospitaller, though they soon left.
banate-of-severin.r: A royal ban commanded the castle and the border, collecting tribute from the Romanian voivodes and knezes beyond, such as the Voivodeship of Litovoi. Control shifted repeatedly with Bulgaria and later the Principality of Wallachia, whose rulers took the title ban of Severin. In the 15th century Hungary held it against the Ottomans, and John Hunyadi was ban.
banate-of-severin.e: Ottoman raids steadily wore it down. Severin fortress fell to the Ottomans in 1524, two years before Mohács, and the banate ceased to exist. The region passed to Wallachia as Oltenia's western edge.

brigantes.t: The largest British confederation, ruling much of northern England under Queen Cartimandua until Rome conquered it after a civil war in the 70s.
brigantes.o: The Brigantes were a grouping of many communities across the Pennines and northern England, from the Mersey and Humber to the Tyne. Their name is linked to the goddess Brigantia. By the time of the Roman invasion of 43 they were under the rule of Queen Cartimandua, who made a treaty with Rome and governed as a client ruler.
brigantes.r: The confederation was loosely held, combining upland pastoralists and lowland farmers, and had no coinage of its own. Its political centre may have been at Stanwick in North Yorkshire, where vast earthwork enclosures were built in the 1st century. Cartimandua handed the fugitive Caratacus to the Romans in 51, and later her divorce from her consort Venutius split the Brigantes into rival factions.
brigantes.e: In 69 Venutius drove Cartimandua out, and Roman troops could only rescue her. Petillius Cerialis then conquered the Brigantes from 71, with the legion based at York. The southern territory became a civitas centred on Isurium Brigantum, Aldborough, in Roman Britain.

bastuli.t: A mixed Iberian and Phoenician people of the coast between Gibraltar and Almería, known to Greek writers as the Blastophoenicians.
bastuli.o: The Bastuli lived along the southern coast of Iberia, roughly from the Strait of Gibraltar to Almería, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Ancient writers called them Bastuli-Poeni or Blastophoenicians, reflecting a population mixing native people with Phoenician and Punic settlers of towns such as Malaka, Sexi and Abdera.
bastuli.r: They lived from farming, fishing and fish salting, and their region minted coins in a distinctive Libyphoenician script. Little is known about their government, and it is debated whether they formed a people at all or were a label for the coastal Punicised communities.
bastuli.e: After the Roman conquest of the south in 206 BCE they came under Hispania Ulterior and took part in the revolt of 197 BCE. Later they were absorbed into Baetica.

bastetani.t: An Iberian people of the Granada highlands, whose capital Basti yielded the seated stone goddess known as the Lady of Baza.
bastetani.o: The Bastetani occupied the uplands of eastern Andalusia, in modern Granada, Almería and Jaén, from the mid-first millennium BCE. Their main town was Basti, near Baza, and they bordered the Oretani, Contestani and coastal Bastuli.
bastetani.r: They lived in fortified towns on hills controlling routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Their elites were buried in rich chamber tombs, as at Tútugi (Galera) and Basti, where the Lady of Baza, a painted stone statue of an enthroned woman used as a cinerary urn, was found in 1971. Their economy combined farming, herding and esparto working.
bastetani.e: After Carthaginian control, the Bastetani passed under Rome during the Second Punic War and joined the great revolt of 197 BCE before being pacified. Their region was divided between Hispania Citerior and Baetica in Roman times.

bailiwick-of-jersey.t: The largest Channel Island, a self-governing Crown Dependency that has stayed loyal to the English crown since the loss of Normandy in 1204.
bailiwick-of-jersey.o: Jersey was part of the Duchy of Normandy from 933. After King John lost mainland Normandy in 1204, the island remained with the English crown and became a separate bailiwick under a warden, later a lieutenant governor, with a bailiff heading its Royal Court.
bailiwick-of-jersey.r: Jersey kept Norman customary law and its own States assembly. Mont Orgueil Castle defended it against frequent French attacks. The island traded in cod from Newfoundland, knitted woollens and later potatoes and cattle, and grew into a financial centre. Charles II was proclaimed king there in 1649, and the French were defeated at the Battle of Jersey in 1781.
bailiwick-of-jersey.e: Germany occupied Jersey from 1940 to 1945. Today it is a Crown Dependency outside the United Kingdom, with its own parliament, the States Assembly, and its own laws and taxes.

bastarnae.t: Probably Germanic people of the lower Danube and Carpathians who fought for Macedon against Rome and later joined the Goths.
bastarnae.o: The Bastarnae appeared north of the lower Danube around 200 BCE, the first Germanic-speaking people known to Greek and Roman writers, though some ancient authors thought them Celts. One branch, the Peucini, lived on the island of Peuce in the Danube delta.
bastarnae.r: They were a warlike confederation of tribes, valued as mercenaries. Philip V and Perseus of Macedon recruited them against Rome, and the Zarubintsy and Poienești-Lukashevka archaeological cultures are often linked to them. In 62 BCE they defeated Gaius Antonius Hybrida near Histria. In 29 BCE Marcus Licinius Crassus defeated them and killed their king Deldo in single combat.
bastarnae.e: Under the empire they remained a frontier people, joining the Goths and Carpi in 3rd-century raids. Around 280 the emperor Probus settled a large number of Bastarnae in Thrace, after which they disappear as a distinct people.

black-sea-cossack-host.t: A Cossack army formed from former Zaporozhians, which settled the Kuban frontier and founded the city now called Krasnodar.
black-sea-cossack-host.o: In 1787, on the eve of war with the Ottoman Empire, Prince Grigory Potemkin gathered former Zaporozhian Cossacks into the Host of Loyal Zaporozhians. Led by Sydir Bilyi, Zakhary Chepiha and Anton Holovaty, they fought at Ochakiv and Izmail, and in 1790 they were renamed the Black Sea Cossack Host.
black-sea-cossack-host.r: In 1792 Catherine II granted the Host the lands of the Taman peninsula and the right bank of the Kuban, and in 1793 they founded Yekaterinodar as their capital. The Cossacks kept elected officers and a Zaporozhian tradition, farming and guarding a fortified line against the Circassians across the Kuban.
black-sea-cossack-host.e: The Host fought throughout the Caucasian War. In 1860 it was merged with part of the Caucasus Line Cossack Host to form the Kuban Cossack Host. Its Ukrainian heritage shaped the speech and culture of the Kuban region.

byblos.t: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician port on the Lebanese coast that shipped cedar to Egypt for over two thousand years and gave the Greeks their word for papyrus.
byblos.o: Gubla, as its people called it, is among the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world. By c. 2600 BCE it had become a walled city whose harbour supplied cedar and resin from the Lebanon mountains to the pharaohs of the Old Kingdom of Egypt, receiving gold, linen and papyrus in return.
byblos.r: Kings ruled under the protection of the city's goddess, the Baalat Gebal, whose temple received Egyptian offerings. In the 14th century BCE its king Rib-Hadda sent dozens of the Amarna letters begging Egypt for help. The sarcophagus of King Ahiram bears one of the earliest inscriptions in the Phoenician alphabet, which Byblos helped to shape.
byblos.e: Byblos lost commercial leadership to Tyre and Sidon in the Iron Age and paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire, the Chaldean Empire and the Achaemenid Empire in turn. It submitted peacefully to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE, ending its independent kingship. The town of Jbeil still occupies the site.
